## Who I am, and why this talk {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
I am a Professor of Urban Analytics at UCL's Centre for Advanced Spatial
Analysis. I build spatial models — of migration, of housing, of how people
move around cities.

I am also a parent in Brighton & Hove, a city that spent 2024 arguing
bitterly about which children should go to which secondary school.

I built the first version of that model myself, by hand, during the 2024
consultation. Two years later I rebuilt it with an AI collaborator — and it
became something I could not have built alone.

**This talk is about which parts were which.**
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: key-finding
This talk is not "I used AI to write my code". It is an attempt to describe
honestly what a research collaboration with an AI system actually looked
like — with the receipts.
:::

Part of the **AI for Collective Intelligence** hub's interest in how AI
changes the practice of applied research.
:::
:::::

## What exists now {.smaller}

| The thing | Scale |
|:--|:--|
| A strategic analysis of the city's school system | 9,712 lines of Quarto |
| A technical guide auditing every model term | 4,736 lines |
| The model itself, plus data assembly | ~7,400 lines of R |
| An interactive policy simulator (Shiny) | ~3,000 lines |
| A private analysis repository | ~8,200 lines |
| Three slide decks | ~3,500 lines |
| Commits across six repositories | 805 |

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
A production-constrained spatial interaction model with a competing-destinations
term, calibrated per catchment, fitted against the council's published offer
data. It reproduces the September 2026 allocations with an R² of 0.95.
:::

## This did not start in April {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
**October 2024.** Brighton & Hove is consulting on redrawing its catchments.
I write `BrighonSchoolsSIM.qmd` — **1,014 lines** of R and Quarto. A
production-constrained spatial interaction model of the city's schools.

I call the hypothetical baseline **Brightopia**: where every child would go
if distance were the only thing that mattered.

**December 2024.** I write `bus_routes.qmd` — **1,021 lines** — setting up
`r5r`, a GTFS feed and an OSM extract to compute real public-transport
journey times to every school.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: key-finding
Two thousand lines of spatial interaction modelling and routing, written by
hand, eighteen months before any of this.
:::

That is what the new model was built **on**, not instead of. Brightopia is
still in the current document, as the $W_j = 1$ baseline the calibrated
model is measured against.

I have been building models like this for twenty years. That is why I knew
what to ask for.
:::
:::::

## The record I am drawing on {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Claude Code keeps a transcript of every session: every instruction I typed,
every action it took, timestamped.

For this talk I parsed **~250 MB of those logs** across ten sessions, plus
the git history of six repositories.

So the numbers that follow are counted, not remembered. They are also
**a snapshot** — the work is still going.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: key-finding
**1,277** instructions from me.

**13,451** tool calls from Claude.

**69** working days, spread over 166.
:::

About **ten and a half actions for every sentence I typed**.
:::
:::::

## Five months, in one chart

```{r fig-timeline}
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
ggplot(rec, aes(day)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = tool_calls), fill = BRIGHT, width = 1.9, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = instructions * 10), colour = WARM, linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "31") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Claude tool calls per day",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / 10, name = "My instructions per day")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       title = "The work was bursty, and it accelerated",
       subtitle = "Bars: actions taken by Claude. Dashed line: instructions from me.") +
  theme_talk(14) +
  theme(axis.title.y.right = element_text(colour = WARM),
        axis.title.y.left  = element_text(colour = BRIGHT))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
The April–July work is a different project — a national school attainment
model. The Brighton system model starts on **8 September** and is finished
eighteen days later.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}
The largest single category is not writing code. It is **running code and
reading the result** — the loop that turns a plausible script into a correct one.
:::

## The division of labour {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What I brought**

- **The working prototype** — Brightopia, and the `r5r` routing pipeline,
  both written by hand in 2024
- Twenty years of building spatial interaction models: knowing that
  attractiveness, distance decay and competing destinations were the terms
  that mattered
- Knowledge of the school system, and of the city's politics
- Judgement about what is defensible to publish
- Knowing when an answer was wrong
- Every decision about what to do next
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What Claude brought**

- Scale: a hand-built prototype turned into a calibrated, audited system
- Data wrangling across a dozen published sources
- Shiny, deployment, rendering, version control
- Debugging, and the patience for it
- Documentation written as it went
- The willingness to redo all of it when one assumption changed
:::
:::::

::: key-finding
I knew what to ask for and what to examine, because I had built a smaller
version of it myself. **That is not a small part of why this worked.**
:::

## What the instructions actually look like {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.82em"}
Verbatim, from the logs. The counts are the tool calls that followed.
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
> **"fonts as well"**
>
> *13 characters → 58 actions*

> **"yes, build it"**
>
> *13 characters → 46 actions*

> **"yes, add Priory, Seahaven and Seaford Head as destinations"**
>
> *58 characters → 68 actions*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> **"Can you cite the sources and link to all of the data that is used in
> each section please then commit and push as I'm going to bed"**
>
> *128 characters → 52 actions*

::: key-finding
Median instruction: **199 characters**. About thirty-six words.
:::
:::
:::::

## But the short ones only work if you know what to say {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
> **"You need to update Figure 28 with the new model outputs. Also, can I
> have a table of the original Brightopia ($W_j = 1$) model with the observed
> vs modelled expected numbers for each school"**

> **"can I have a little section on how we arrived at the best $W_j$
> attractiveness factor — we end up using Attainment 8"**

> **"can you just check whether the shared variance issues make a difference
> here? I don't think they do, but it might be worth checking using the
> Shapley work"**
:::

::: key-finding
These are instructions written in the language of the model. You cannot
issue them unless you already know what $W_j$ is, why it might be wrong, and
what would count as checking.
:::

## The routing, as it actually happened {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
I was running `r5r` myself. It broke:

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
> **"`Error in purrr::map(): Caused by error in checkmate::assert_class():
> argument "r5r_network" is missing`"**
:::

Then, an hour later:

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}
> **"restarted R and re-ran, it's routing now — we now have a brand new
> travel matrix — can we now go back to the original analysis and re-run the
> models with the new travel matrix? Both the public and private analyses"**
>
> *213 characters → 35 actions*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: key-finding
This is the collaboration in one exchange. I built and debugged the routing
pipeline. It took the output and propagated it through every model, every
document and every figure that depended on it.
:::

Neither of us could have done the other's half quickly.
:::
:::::

## Worked example: a school in the wrong place {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The model had Hove Park School at its Nevill Road site. Reasonable — that is
the address in the published data.

Five months in, I realised: the school has operated **two campuses**. Year 7
and 8 were at the Valley Campus, a mile away, until a closure proposal in 2026.

The model had been calibrated on the wrong location for the children who
actually generate the demand.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: key-finding
No amount of code quality would have caught this. It needed someone who
knew the city.
:::

Re-calibrating moved about **a quarter of Hove Park's modelled intake**
between wards, and changed the disadvantage figures materially.
:::
:::::

## What re-calibrating it showed {.smaller}

```{r fig-hovepark}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
mv <- hpc$move |>
  select(year, Valley = valley, `Nevill Road` = nevill) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "site", values_to = "intake")
ggplot(mv, aes(factor(year), intake, fill = site)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), width = 0.66) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(intake)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), vjust = -0.5,
            size = 4.4, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Valley = GREY, `Nevill Road` = BRIGHT)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 205)) +
  labs(x = "Entry year", y = "Modelled Year 7 intake",
       title = "The same school, half a mile apart",
       subtitle = "Modelled intake with Hove Park at the Valley Campus, and consolidated at Nevill Road") +
  theme_talk(14)
```

::: key-finding
Moving site is worth about **twelve extra children a year** — roughly a 7%
lift, from geography alone. Real, but far smaller than the school's
attractiveness. The question "is it the site or the reputation?" now has a
number attached.
:::

## Worked example: the simulator {.smaller}

![](slides_assets/simulator-front.png){fig-align="center" width="74%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}
Every scenario in this talk is a control in here. Built in about two days,
and the reason the "what if" questions became cheap enough to ask twenty
times instead of twice.
:::

## Worked example: a question only a human asks {.smaller}

Families choose schools on the published Attainment 8 score — which mostly
measures the intake, not the teaching.

I asked: **what if they chose on value added instead?**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
That is not a coding task. It is a question about how a city might behave
differently, and it took about a day to answer properly: a new attractiveness
basis, a switch in the simulator, a measure of how evenly children would be
spread.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: key-finding
The answer: one struggling school's intake nearly doubles, the surplus stops
concentrating in three schools — and the total number of empty places does
not move at all.
:::
:::
:::::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
Brighton Aldridge — the lowest Attainment 8 in the city — is adding more
progress than almost anywhere. Patcham, comfortably mid-table on the
headline number, is bottom of the city on value added.
:::

## Worked example: catching it being wrong {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
Claude reported a school's value-added score as being in the "top 100% in
England". It had applied an Attainment 8 percentile function to a
value-added figure. Silently wrong, confidently stated.

Later, the attainment charts appeared to show huge jumps when the
value-added option was selected — because they were reading a different
variable than I thought.

I caught both. It fixed both in minutes.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: key-finding
The failure mode is not gibberish. It is **plausible, well-formatted,
confidently-presented wrongness** — exactly what a domain expert catches
and a non-expert does not.
:::

This is the strongest argument I have for why the human in this loop has to
be someone who knows the subject.
:::
:::::

## The other failure modes, honestly {.smaller}

| What went wrong | What it cost |
|:--|:--|
| A shell quoting slip corrupted two files | 20 minutes, fixed by regenerating |
| An optimiser fell into the wrong basin | Caught by a sanity check on one school's intake |
| A variable name collision inside the app | Silent wrong behaviour until tested |
| Model outputs stale after re-calibration | Needed a discipline of re-running everything |
| Confident summaries of work not yet verified | Needed me to ask "did you actually check?" |

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}
None of these are exotic. They are the ordinary failure modes of a fast,
capable, over-confident collaborator — and they are managed the same way you
manage those in a person: tests, checks, and someone reading the output.
:::

## The workflow {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Everything is **Quarto**. The analysis document, the technical guide, the
slide decks — all `.qmd`, all executing live R against the same data.

The loop, many times a day:

1. I say what I want, usually in two or three sentences
2. Claude edits the source and runs it
3. It renders, screenshots, checks the numbers
4. It commits and pushes
5. I read the rendered output and react
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: key-finding
The document **is** the analysis. There is no separate "writing up" —
changing the model changes the paragraph that describes it, because the
paragraph is generated from the model.
:::

Git is the memory. 805 commits, each with a message explaining why.
:::
:::::

## Why Quarto matters more than it sounds {.smaller}

When I asked "does the Hove Park change affect section 5.5?", that was
answerable — because section 5.5 is code, and the code re-runs.

When I asked for the deck to be rebuilt with the new numbers, no one had to
re-type any numbers.

::: key-finding
Reproducibility stops being a virtue you aspire to and becomes the only way
the thing can work at this speed. If the outputs were hand-copied into Word,
none of this would survive its own rate of change.
:::

## The recursion {.smaller}

The interesting part is not that it wrote code. It is the **loop**:

::: incremental
1. A model produces a result.
2. The result goes into a document, written to be read by councillors.
3. Writing it clearly exposes a hole in the argument.
4. The hole becomes a new question for the model.
5. Answering it changes the model — and the document rewrites itself.
:::

. . .

That cycle ran perhaps two hundred times. Each turn took minutes, not weeks.
**That compression is the whole story.**

## Eighteen days {.smaller}

```{r fig-sept}

ggplot(sept, aes(day, tool_calls)) +
  geom_col(fill = BRIGHT, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = tool_calls), vjust = -0.5, size = 4.2, colour = INK) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 days", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1300)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tool calls",
       title = "From nothing to a working city model",
       subtitle = "8 September: first commit. 26 September: model, site, simulator, three decks.") +
  theme_talk(14)
```

## What I would say to a colleague {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**It does not replace knowing things.** Every moment that mattered in this
project turned on domain knowledge I had and it did not.

**It does collapse the cost of trying.** The scenarios I tested would each
have been a week of work. Testing twenty of them was previously impossible,
so I would have tested two.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**It writes better documentation than I do**, because it never gets bored
of writing it.

**It needs supervision that looks like peer review**, not like proofreading.

**The bottleneck moved.** It is no longer implementation. It is knowing
which question is worth asking.
:::
:::::

## Open questions {.smaller}

::: incremental
- **Authorship.** What is the honest way to describe this on a paper? I directed
  every step and verified every output — but I did not write the code.
- **Verification at speed.** I can generate analysis faster than I can
  properly check it. That is a new kind of risk.
- **Reproducibility of the process.** The code is reproducible. The
  *conversation* that produced it is not, in any meaningful sense.
- **Who else can do this?** This worked because I could tell right from wrong.
  What happens when the person in the loop cannot?
:::
